subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: The role and functions of education
Sociological theories of education (functionalism and Marxism)

questions.q: Which functionalist sociologist argued that education transmits society's shared norms and values, creating 'social solidarity'?
questions.explain: Durkheim saw education as passing on shared culture and binding individuals into society through social solidarity.

questions.q: What sociological term describes how schools teach children the wider norms and values of society beyond the family?
questions.explain: Secondary socialisation is the learning of society's norms and values by agencies such as schools, beyond the family.

questions.q: Parsons described the school as a 'bridge'. A bridge between what?
questions.explain: Parsons argued school bridges the family and wider society by moving pupils from particularistic to universalistic standards.

questions.q: What does it mean to describe education as 'meritocratic'?
options: Rewards and positions are earned through ability and effort
Teachers select pupils by social background
questions.explain: A meritocracy allocates rewards on the basis of talent and hard work rather than birth or privilege.

questions.q: Which function of education involves 'sifting and sorting' pupils into suitable future roles and jobs?
questions.explain: Functionalists argue education sorts pupils by ability and allocates them to appropriate roles in the division of labour.

questions.q: Which sociologists are associated with the Marxist view of education and the 'correspondence principle'?
questions.explain: Bowles and Gintis argued schooling mirrors the workplace, reproducing an obedient, exploitable workforce.

questions.q: What is meant by the 'hidden curriculum'?
options: The informal lessons and values pupils learn indirectly at school
The subjects timetabled but not examined
A secret syllabus known only to teachers
The exam content withheld until the test
questions.explain: The hidden curriculum refers to unofficial learning such as obedience, punctuality and acceptance of hierarchy.

questions.q: Marxists argue that meritocracy is a 'myth'. What do they mean?
options: Success is really shaped by class background, not just ability
Nobody can ever succeed through education
Meritocracy only applies to private schools
questions.explain: Marxists claim the 'myth of meritocracy' hides how education reproduces class inequality across generations.

questions.q: The 'correspondence principle' claims that school life corresponds to what?
questions.explain: Bowles and Gintis argued the routines and hierarchies of school mirror those of the capitalist workplace.

questions.q: A school rewards pupils for arriving on time, wearing uniform and obeying without question. A Marxist would MOST likely interpret this as:
options: The hidden curriculum preparing pupils to accept workplace discipline
Effective secondary socialisation into shared values
questions.explain: Marxists see such rules as the hidden curriculum producing a docile, obedient future workforce.

questions.q: Bernstein linked working-class underachievement to the use of which type of language?
questions.explain: Bernstein argued working-class pupils tend to use a restricted code, while schools value the elaborated code.

questions.q: Which concept, associated with Bourdieu, describes the knowledge, tastes and skills of the middle class that are rewarded in school?
questions.explain: Bourdieu argued middle-class children possess cultural capital that gives them an advantage in the education system.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of 'material deprivation' affecting achievement?
options: A family cannot afford a quiet study space or a computer
Parents show little interest in schoolwork
Pupils use a restricted speech code
A pupil is labelled as unintelligent
questions.explain: Material deprivation refers to a lack of physical resources such as space, equipment or money that harms learning.

questions.q: Sophie's parents take her to museums and galleries and help her use formal language valued by teachers. A sociologist would say Sophie benefits from:
questions.explain: Her family's cultural knowledge and language match what schools reward, giving her an advantage (cultural capital).

questions.q: Sue Sharpe's research compared girls' priorities in the 1970s and 1990s. What key change did she identify?
options: Girls shifted from prioritising marriage to prioritising careers and qualifications
Girls became less interested in education
Girls began to underachieve compared with boys
questions.explain: Sharpe found girls' ambitions moved away from marriage towards jobs, careers and being self-reliant.

questions.q: Amara says she wants a professional career and good qualifications rather than to marry young. This attitude best illustrates which explanation for girls' improved achievement?
options: Changing ambitions and aspirations among girls
questions.explain: Rising female aspirations, as noted by Sharpe, are used to explain girls' improved educational performance.

questions.q: What is meant by an 'ethnocentric curriculum'?
options: A curriculum that prioritises one culture, often the majority white British culture
A curriculum focused only on ethnic minority histories
A curriculum with no religious content
questions.explain: An ethnocentric curriculum reflects the culture of the dominant group and can disadvantage minority ethnic pupils.

questions.q: Which sociologist studied how teachers label pupils against an image of the 'ideal pupil'?
questions.explain: Becker found teachers judge pupils against an 'ideal pupil' image, often influenced by class and behaviour.

questions.q: What does the 'self-fulfilling prophecy' describe in education?
options: A label leads a pupil to behave in line with it, making it come true
Pupils predicting their own exam grades accurately
A pupil ignoring a teacher's label
questions.explain: When pupils internalise a teacher's label, their performance can change to match it, fulfilling the prediction.

questions.q: A group of boys studied by Willis reject school rules, mess around and value 'having a laff'. This group is an example of:
questions.explain: Willis's 'lads' formed an anti-school subculture that rejected the school's values and rewards.
